newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Defector says North Korea plans war, no nuclear proof.
newsitem.headline: Defector says North Korea plans war, no nuclear proof.

text.p: The highest ranking North Korean ever to flee his homeland said repeatedly on Thursday that Pyongyang was preparing for war, but that he had no proof it had nuclear weapons.
"The North's war preparation is beyond imagination," Hwang Jang-yop said, describing the entire country as a fortress with tunnels and underground military facilities.

On arrival in Seoul on April 20, he declared his mission was to stop Pyongyang from launching war as a desperate way out of hunger and economic collapse. He said Pyongyang could scorch South Korea, and even Japan, in a nuclear attack.
But on Thursday, after lengthy debriefing by South Korean intelligence officials, he conceded he had no concrete evidence to back up his nuclear claims.
"It is common knowledge they do have these weapons, but there is no means to verify that," he said. "I'm not an expert, so I don't really know."
However, he advised the South "it would be wise" to assume that Pyongyang had nuclear arms.

Washington officials have cast doubt on whether Hwang, an ideologue who helped to author Pyongyang's guiding ideology of self-reliance, or "juche", is in a position to comment on North Korea's nuclear secrets.
Hwang sought asylum at South Korea's Beijing consulate in February, he was stuck for more than two months in China and the Philippines before being spirited to Seoul.
His main themes that North Korea is on a war footing, people are starving and the communist system has turned into a cruel dictatorship caused no surprise at all.
There had been hopes he might give illuminating insights into the state of mind of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il and the North Korean power structure.
But at the news conference he sidestepped questions about Kim, saying issues such as whether Kim had injured himself by falling off a horse, or liked spicy food, were irrelevant.
He predicted that Kim would formally assume leadership of the all-powerful Workers' Party this year.

North Korea on Tuesday declared an end to a three-year mourning period for Kim's father, "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, paving the way for Kim junior to assume the vacant posts of Workers' Party general secretary and state president.

"North Korean society is swept by a war atmosphere," Hwang said, while declining to say when he thought war may break out. The leadership had no other option except to choose between reform and military adventure, he said.
"It is obvious the North has no intention to reform and open, but is only seeking provocation through war.
"In short, the entire land is a fortress," he said.
Pyongyang leaders continued to put on a false show of power despite accepting international food aid after two years of failed crops, he said.

Hwang said the North had been reduced to a "living hell" where starving residents were forced to deify their leader. He hinted at the existence of concentration camps when asked whether North Koreans supported Kim.
If they did, he replied "why are hundreds of thousands of people dying in restricted areas?"
He paid his tribute to South Koreans who he said had achieved a "historic miracle" with rapid economic development.

South Korea's central bank said on Wednesday North Korea's economy shrank for the seventh year in a row in 1996, crippled by shortages of energy and raw materials. Per-capita gross national product dropped to $910 in 1996 from $957 in 1995.
"South and North are like heaven and earth -- they are worlds apart," he said.
Hwang apologised to South Korea for the role he played in building the North Korean system.
"I feel remorse I was part of this regime," he said.
